narrative.text: Front matter of the Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (ISBN 978-92-4-011619-1 electronic, 978-92-4-011620-7 print; © WHO 2025, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO), including suggested citation, CIP data, licensing terms, general disclaimers, and the table of contents.

Acknowledges WHO leadership (Alain Labrique, Garrett Mehl, Deusdedit Mubangizi, Fred Were, Carl Leitner), principal contributors (Sherri Haas, Venu Madhav Garikipati), external experts and WHO staff from the Kigali Technical Workshops (December 2023 and April 2024), and financial support from USAID and the Gates Foundation.

Structured table of 43 abbreviations and acronyms used across the handbook, including AEFI (printed in source as 'Adverse effects following immunisation'; note WHO standard expansion is 'Adverse events following immunization', tracked in litlfred/smart-ra#142), AIDC, ATC, DAK, DHSC, DIIG, eLMIS, FHIR, GDSN, GTIN, HL7, ICD-11, ICHI, IDMP, INN, NAFDAC, NPC, NRA, OpenHIE, PCMT, SMART, TSS, UMC, WHODrug, WMS, ZAMMSA, and ZAMRA.

Structured glossary table defining 17 core terms: Data element, Digitization, Digitalization, Digital transformation, End user, Features, Functional requirements, Generic product or product information, Interoperability, Non-functional requirements, Open source, Open standards, Organogram, Registry, SMART Guidelines, Trade item, and User acceptance testing (UAT).

Introduces product master data and its role in digital health supply chains (Fig. 1–3), alignment with the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG, Fig. 4), WHO SMART Guidelines L1–L5 knowledge layers and ANC workflow connections (Fig. 5–6), the Digital Health Supply Chain (DHSC) architecture framework (Fig. 7), handbook methodology, target users across Chapters 1–7, and scenarios for using the handbook.

Chapter 1 overview explaining the role of Ministries of Health and National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) in establishing policies and legislation that mandate manufacturers and distributors to supply standardized product master data.

Chapter 1, Step 1: Structured step table (inputs, steps, resources, outputs) and risk/mitigation table for analysing existing regulations, assessing compliance mechanisms, and identifying required regulatory policies and legislative updates for product master data standardization.

Chapter 1, Step 2: Structured step table for drafting master data guidelines and product identification/labelling regulations aligned with data standardization and AIDC standards, including phased roll-out timelines for manufacturer compliance.

Chapter 1, Step 3: Structured step table and risk/mitigation table for evaluating drafted regulatory policies with public and private sector stakeholders, addressing feedback, and obtaining formal approvals.

Chapter 1, Step 4: Structured step table, risk/mitigation table, and Chapter 1 checkpoint for publishing approved master data policies and defining mechanisms to institutionalize and monitor manufacturer compliance.
Chapter 2 overview on establishing product master data management policies, structures, definitions, and governance procedures to sustain data integrity, quality, privacy, and security.

Chapter 2, Step 1: Structured step table for assessing existing master data challenges and harmonization needs, together with detailed elements of master data management procedures (data governance roles of Data owner, Data custodian, and Data steward, quality management, security, interoperability, lifecycle, change management, and monitoring).

Chapter 2, Step 2: Structured step table and risk/mitigation table for defining standardized coding schemes and data structures, linkage across classifications, generic products, trade items, and regulated trade items (Fig. 8), HL7 FHIR three-class data model with attribute cardinalities (Fig. 9), coding best practices, WHODrug reference dictionary, GS1 packaging hierarchy (Fig. 10), manufacturer packaging variations (Fig. 11), and HL7 FHIR InventoryItem packaging hierarchy mapping (Fig. 12).

Chapter 2, Step 3: Structured step table and risk/mitigation table for identifying master data sources and consumers, determining secure data sharing mechanisms, and establishing ethical data use and data sharing policies.

Chapter 2, Step 4: Structured step table for establishing a multi-stakeholder master data governance group and integrating master data management procedures, coding schemes, and governance policies across health supply chain operations.

Chapter 2, Step 5: Structured step table, risk/mitigation table, and Chapter 2 checkpoint for defining short-, medium-, and long-term strategies to source standardized product master data (from packaging/donors initially to formal regulatory registration submissions).
Chapter 3 overview on selecting and implementing an appropriate technology tool to establish and maintain a National Product Catalogue (NPC) with minimal manual intervention.

Chapter 3, Step 1: Structured step table for defining and approving functional and non-functional system requirements for an NPC tool aligned with Target Software Standards (TSS), ISO IDMP, and HL7 FHIR.

Chapter 3, Step 2: Structured step table for conducting market research (RFI/RFQ/RFP), assessing existing enterprise tools, evaluating open-source options (such as PCMT and the WHO-hosted PCMT), and selecting an NPC technology tool.
Chapter 3, Step 3: Structured step table for developing and reviewing a detailed NPC implementation project plan to design, configure, deploy, and integrate the chosen NPC tool.

Chapter 3, Step 4: Structured step table, risk/mitigation table, and Chapter 3 checkpoint for designing, configuring, integrating, validating (system, integration, performance testing, and UAT), hosting, and deploying the NPC tool.
Chapter 4 overview on change management procedures to transition operational processes, systems, and personnel to standardized product master data without disrupting existing operations.

Chapter 4, Step 1: Structured step table for developing a change management plan across people, processes, and systems, plus best practices and structured tables for transitioning from local Country Trade Item Identifiers to globally unique GS1 GTINs (Fig. 13).

Chapter 4, Step 2: Structured step table, risk/mitigation/resources table, and Chapter 4 checkpoint for defining, validating, and approving product master data management SOPs and institutionalizing a continuous training and advocacy plan.
Chapter 5 overview on building sustainable human resource capacity and technical/operational skills to manage the NPC system, processes, and data.

Chapter 5, Step 1: Structured step table for determining human resource capacity requirements, identifying operational and technical roles (such as Catalogue Manager and NPC System Administrator), defining job descriptions, and updating the human resource management plan.
Chapter 5, Step 2: Structured step table for developing budgets, identifying funding sources, and recruiting, onboarding, and training personnel for identified NPC roles.

Chapter 5, Step 3: Structured step table and Chapter 5 checkpoint for developing a knowledge management plan, resource organogram, and governmental strategy to engage and enable local vendors and implementation partners.

Chapter 6: Describes the WHO-hosted Product Catalogue Management Tool (PCMT) (available in 2026), its conceptual architecture linking the WHO Global Catalogue with Country Catalogues A and B (Fig. 14), and its user-group/category access permission model (`WHOGroup`, `CAGroup`, `CBGroup`), cross-catalogue associations, and copy rules.

Chapter 7: Explains the value of sharing national product master data as a global good with the WHO Global Product Catalogue (accurate information, standardization, reduced redundancy, crisis management, equal access, capacity building) and presents the bidirectional data-sharing model across countries and the WHO-hosted PCMT (Fig. 15).

Chapter 8: Structured comparative implementation experience tables for Rwanda, Zambia, and Nigeria across five dimensions (Regulatory, Data, Technology, People, Change Management) and five rows (Status, Process, Challenges, Approaches adopted, Best-practices/lessons learnt).

Lists the 17 numbered bibliographic references cited across the handbook, covering digitization/digitalization/digital transformation, UNIDO standards, WHO SMART Guidelines, open-source licensing, ITU open standards, GS1 GTINs, UAT, the WHO Digital Transformation Handbook for Health Supply Chain Architecture, and the Principles for Digital Development.

Annex 1: Structured table of the 9 Principles for Digital Development (Understand the existing ecosystem; Share, reuse, and improve; Design with people; Design for inclusion; Build for sustainability; Establish people-first data practices; Create open and transparent practices; Anticipate and mitigate harms; Use evidence to improve outcomes).

Annex 2: Structured matrix of technical and leadership roles for NPC implementation (Project manager, Solution architect, Business analyst, Developer/programmers, Integration specialist, Database administrator, Infrastructure specialist, QA/test manager, Test analyst, System administrator, Support engineer, Superuser/trainer) detailing deployment/operation phases, position type, skill sets, and responsibilities.
